alalal-e78451-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 5: whether unformed faith is a virtue.

alalal-e78451-d1e111.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's words 'for that which is believed, and is not a virtue'.

alalal-e78451-d1e123.summary: Notes that this implies unformed faith is not a virtue, which the text seems to prove.

alalal-e78451-d1e133.summary: Introduces arguments from reason for the same conclusion.

alalal-e78451-d1e138.summary: First argument: a dead man is not a man; unformed faith is dead, so it is not faith.

alalal-e78451-d1e149.summary: Second argument: something unformed in a species is called by the generic name only if it has the form of another species of that genus; unformed faith lacks faith's form and has no other virtue's form, so it cannot be called a virtue.

alalal-e78451-d1e184.summary: Third argument: virtue is a good quality by which one lives rightly, which no one misuses, which God works in us without us (Augustine); unformed faith coexists with the stain of sin and many who have it do not live rightly.

alalal-e78451-d1e217.summary: Fourth argument: Augustine says virtue is a quality by which one lives the spiritual life; one does not live by unformed faith.

alalal-e78451-d1e231.summary: Fifth argument: if a virtue, it is infused or acquired; if infused and ordering to the end like theological virtues, it would make one pleasing to God, which is absurd for the worst sinners; if it is a gratuitously given grace, then as such it is not a virtue, like prophecy or the word of wisdom.
concepts: gratia gratum faciens vs gratis data

alalal-e78451-d1e271.summary: Sed contra: virtues are defined by their acts; Cicero's definition of virtue fits unformed faith, which, lacking sufficient reason, consents in the manner of nature; so it is a virtue.

alalal-e78451-d1e297.summary: Second sed contra: many virtues are common to the good and the wicked, since only charity divides the children of the kingdom from those of perdition; so coexistence with sin does not disqualify it.
concepts: virtues common to good and bad

alalal-e78451-d1e317.summary: Third sed contra: believing what is not apparent exceeds reason, believing the apparent is below it, so a virtue other than reason is needed for the former, and unformed faith is the only candidate.

alalal-e78451-d1e335.summary: Solution: virtue as 'disposition of the perfect to the best' is said by priority and posteriority: first of gratuitous virtues, then of unformed ones, last of acquired virtues, which are the most remote dispositions to the best. So unformed faith is a virtue, but without the complete ratio of virtue that formed faith or other virtues making one pleasing have.
claims: Unformed faith is a virtue in a secondary, incomplete sense.

alalal-e78451-d1e366.summary: Reply to the first argument: unformed faith is not dead in the sense of lacking the potency for life, but because its subject is unfit to receive the life of faith from God; the cause of its death is outside it, so it retains the relation to virtue, unlike a dead man.
claims: Unformed faith is 'dead' because its subject lacks charity, not because it lacks the potency for life.

alalal-e78451-d1e392.summary: Reply to the second: faith is called unformed by lack of the form giving virtue's perfection, not by lack of species, otherwise it would not be faith. That form, discussed later, is perfection in the power to reach the end rather than in the being of the species, so unformed faith has the species and admits the predication of the genus.
claims: Unformed faith has the species of faith but lacks the form that perfects it toward the end.

alalal-e78451-d1e424.summary: Reply to the third: faith is a good quality, though without the complete goodness that excludes sin; it is called good because of itself it opposes sin, and of itself one lives rightly by it.

alalal-e78451-d1e440.summary: Reply to the fourth: the spiritual life is the act of a virtue only when joined to grace, since grace is the life of the soul; Augustine's dictum concerns infused virtue with grace.
concepts: grace as life of the soul

alalal-e78451-d1e453.summary: Reply to the fifth: faith is a virtue infused by God and a gift of the Spirit in the broad sense. Being a gratuitously given grace that does not make one pleasing does not prevent it from being a virtue, since graces that order life toward God, like servile fear and unformed faith, have the ratio of virtue, though not the most complete.
claims: Unformed faith is an infused gift ordering life toward God and so has the ratio of virtue.

alalal-e78451.summary: Article 5 asks whether unformed faith is a virtue, as Lombard's text seems to deny. Arguments against cite its 'death', its lack of form, Augustine's definitions of virtue, and the dilemma that it would either make sinners pleasing to God or be a mere gratuitous grace. Arguments for note that it fits Cicero's definition, that only charity divides the saved from the damned, and that believing beyond reason requires a distinct virtue. Albert holds that 'virtue', as a disposition of the perfect to the best, is said by priority: first of gratuitous virtues, then of unformed ones, last of acquired ones. Unformed faith is a virtue in a secondary sense. It is dead because its subject lacks charity, not through any defect in itself. It has the species of faith but lacks the form perfecting it toward the end. It opposes sin of itself, and as an infused gift ordering life to God it has the ratio of virtue, though incompletely.
claims: Unformed faith is a virtue in a secondary, incomplete sense.
Unformed faith retains the species of faith but lacks the form that perfects it toward the end.
The 'death' of unformed faith comes from its subject's lack of charity, not from faith itself.
